items.readable_text:
Content:
Often, differential equations aren't easy to solve. Some are so difficult that they can only be solved using entire rooms full of very powerful computers!

Content:
However, there is one type that's often quite easy. These are differential equations that can be written as

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = g(x).]

Content:
As an example, suppose that we want to find the solution to

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{1}{1+2x}.]

Content:
We can solve this differential equation by integrating both sides:

Content:
[MATH: \int\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\,\textrm d x = \int\dfrac{1}{1+2x}\,\textrm d x]

Content:
For the left-hand side, calculating the indefinite integral of [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}] gives [MATH: y+C_1] because differentiation is reversed by integration. For the right-hand side, this is a reasonably standard integral that we know how to compute. So, we get

Content:
[MATH: y + C_1 = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln|1+2x| + C_2.]

Content:
We now tidy up the result, solving for [MATH: y] and combining the two constants [MATH: C_1] and [MATH: C_2] into a third constant [MATH: C=C_2-C_1.]

Content:
[MATH: y + C_{1}|= (1)/(2)\ln|1 + 2x|+ C_{2}; y|= (1)/(2)\ln|1 + 2x|+ (C_{2} − C_{1}); = (1)/(2)\ln|1 + 2x|+ C]

Content:
The solution we obtained is called a general solution because it involves the arbitrary constant [MATH: C.] This is in contrast to "particular" solutions, in which the constant is set to a fixed value. We will learn more about particular solutions later, but for now we will focus on general solutions.

Content:
Note: Remember that we combined the constants [MATH: C_1] and [MATH: C_2] into a single constant [MATH: C.] For these types of differential equations, we can usually do this, and for that reason, we often go straight to adding a constant [MATH: C] to one side of the equation.

sections.normalized_html: Solve the differential equation [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2} = x.]

Solve the differential equation
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2} = x.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Integrating the equation once, we get [MATH: ∫(d^{2}y)/(dx^{2})dx|= ∫xdx; (dy)/(dx)|= (1)/(2)x^{2} + C.]

Integrating a second time, we get [MATH: ∫(dy)/(dx)dx|= ∫((1)/(2)x^{2} + C)dx; y|= (1)/(6)x^{3} + Cx + D]

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains two arbitrary constants, [MATH: C] and [MATH: D.] We cannot combine them, because [MATH: C] is being multiplied by [MATH: x] while [MATH: D] is not.

items.readable_text:
Content:
Often, instead of the general solution that involves an arbitrary constant, we want a particular solution. A particular solution is a solution that satisfies the differential equation and some other condition on the function.

Content:
As a simple example, consider the differential equation
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx} = 2x.]

Content:
We can find the general solution by integrating:

Content:
[MATH: ∫(dy)/(dx)dx|= ∫2xdx; y|= x^{2} + C.]

Content:
In its current form, the function [MATH: y] represents infinitely many solutions, each with a different value of the arbitrary constant [MATH: C.]

Content:
However, suppose we want to find a particular solution that satisfies the condition [MATH: y(3)=10.] To do this, we can solve for the appropriate value of the arbitrary constant:

Content:
[MATH: y|= x^{2} + C; 10|= 3^{2} + C; 10|= 9 + C; 1|= C.]

Content:
Therefore, the desired particular solution is

Content:
[MATH: y = x^2 + 1.]

sections.normalized_html: Find the particular solution to the differential equation below that satisfies the condition [MATH: f(0)=2.] [MATH: f'(x) - \dfrac{3}{1+x^2} = 0]
sections.readable_text:
Find the particular solution to the differential equation below that satisfies the condition [MATH: f(0)=2.]
[MATH: f'(x) - \dfrac{3}{1+x^2} = 0]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

[MATH: f'(x) = \dfrac{3}{1+x^2}.]

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to [MATH: x,] and get

[MATH: ∫f^{′}(x)dx|= ∫(3)/(1 + x^{2})dx; f(x)|= 3∫(1)/(1 + x^{2})dx; = 3\arctan x + C.]

So our general solution is [MATH: f(x) = 3\arctan{x} + C.] To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition [MATH: f(0) = 2] into our solution and obtain a value for [MATH: C,] as follows:

[MATH: f(x)|= 3\arctan (x) + C; 2|= 3\arctan (0) + C; 2|= 0 + C; C|= 2.]

Therefore, our particular solution is

[MATH: f(x)=3\arctan x + 2.]

Item 5 — Example: Finding the General Solution of a Second Order Differential Equation by Integrating Twice

Example Prompt:
Solve the differential equation
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2} = x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Integrating the equation once, we get
[MATH: ∫(d^{2}y)/(dx^{2})dx|= ∫xdx; (dy)/(dx)|= (1)/(2)x^{2} + C.]

Integrating a second time, we get
[MATH: ∫(dy)/(dx)dx|= ∫((1)/(2)x^{2} + C)dx; y|= (1)/(6)x^{3} + Cx + D]

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains two arbitrary constants, [MATH: C] and [MATH: D.] We cannot combine them, because [MATH: C] is being multiplied by [MATH: x] while [MATH: D] is not.

Item 11 — Tutorial: Particular Solutions of a Differential Equation

Content:
Often, instead of the general solution that involves an arbitrary constant, we want a particular solution. A particular solution is a solution that satisfies the differential equation and some other condition on the function.

Content:
As a simple example, consider the differential equation
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx} = 2x.]

Content:
We can find the general solution by integrating:

Content:
[MATH: ∫(dy)/(dx)dx|= ∫2xdx; y|= x^{2} + C.]

Content:
In its current form, the function [MATH: y] represents infinitely many solutions, each with a different value of the arbitrary constant [MATH: C.]

Content:
However, suppose we want to find a particular solution that satisfies the condition [MATH: y(3)=10.] To do this, we can solve for the appropriate value of the arbitrary constant:

Content:
[MATH: y|= x^{2} + C; 10|= 3^{2} + C; 10|= 9 + C; 1|= C.]

Content:
Therefore, the desired particular solution is

Content:
[MATH: y = x^2 + 1.]

Item 12 — Example: Finding the Solution of a Differential Equation With a Given Condition

Example Prompt:
Find the particular solution to the differential equation below that satisfies the condition [MATH: f(0)=2.]
[MATH: f'(x) - \dfrac{3}{1+x^2} = 0]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

[MATH: f'(x) = \dfrac{3}{1+x^2}.]

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to [MATH: x,] and get

[MATH: ∫f^{′}(x)dx|= ∫(3)/(1 + x^{2})dx; f(x)|= 3∫(1)/(1 + x^{2})dx; = 3\arctan x + C.]

So our general solution is [MATH: f(x) = 3\arctan{x} + C.] To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition [MATH: f(0) = 2] into our solution and obtain a value for [MATH: C,] as follows:

[MATH: f(x)|= 3\arctan (x) + C; 2|= 3\arctan (0) + C; 2|= 0 + C; C|= 2.]

Therefore, our particular solution is

[MATH: f(x)=3\arctan x + 2.]
